investment_summary:
Fair Isaac closed fiscal 2026 with revenue up 27% to $2.53 billion and operating income up 37% to $1.27 billion, driven by Scores [1]. Free cash flow reached $1.03 billion, but $3.05 billion of buybacks were funded largely by $2.2 billion of net new debt, lifting total debt to $5.3 billion [1].

At $707.40 the market capitalisation is about $15.1 billion [2]. Our reverse DCF implies 10.2% annual revenue growth for ten years at the current enterprise value of $20.1 billion. Consensus expects 2.2% growth in FY2027 and 6.5% in FY2028, while historical three-year revenue growth was 18.8% [2][3]. The price therefore requires a decade of near-10% growth, between recent history and current consensus. The implied return of 8.6% is below the 11.5% cost of capital [2][3].

Our view is Hold, consistent with the consensus rating. The franchise is highly profitable, but the main risks are VantageScore adoption in mortgages and rising leverage [1]. Current-year EPS estimates fell 16.5% in 90 days [3].
key_takeaways: Scores should keep carrying earnings in FY2027 as mortgage pricing holds, but that tailwind is exposed to VantageScore: Scores revenue rose 41% [1].
Leverage will limit further buybacks: debt reached 4.2x operating income, and repurchases of $3.05 billion ran well ahead of $1.03 billion free cash flow [1].
The valuation looks demanding, because the reverse DCF needs 10.2% revenue growth for a decade while consensus expects 2.2% for FY2027 [2][3].
Software growth will stay uneven until platform migration offsets legacy decline: platform ARR rose 72% but non-platform ARR fell 18% [1].
business_overview:
Fair Isaac Corporation (NYSE: FICO), founded in 1956, is a global analytics software company. Its best-known product is the FICO Score, the standard U.S. measure of consumer credit risk on a 300 to 850 scale, used in most U.S. credit decisions. The company also sells decisioning software in more than 70 countries [1]. Fiscal 2026 revenue was $2.53 billion, up 27%, split between Scores at $1.65 billion (65%) and Software at $882.7 million (35%) [1]. Scores is the profit engine, and the cost base is light: cost of revenues was $351.5 million against $2.53 billion of revenue [1].

Scores revenue rose 41% on higher unit prices and volume of business-to-business mortgage origination scores, and the segment earned a 90% operating margin, up from 88% [1]. In April 2026 the Federal Housing Finance Agency approved FICO Score 10T for the conforming mortgage market. The company launched the Mortgage Direct License Program in October 2025, which lets distributors bypass the agencies to reduce lender costs [1]. Software revenue grew 7% to $882.7 million. FICO Platform annual recurring revenue (ARR) reached $452.6 million, 53% of the $850.9 million software total and up 72%, while dollar-based net retention was 112% [1]. The filing notes that the market may be unreceptive to the platform approach, so this growth is not assured [1].

The company is also reshaping its cost base and go-to-market approach. It eliminated about 15% of positions in the fourth quarter at a $27.3 million charge, and it is expanding partnerships with systems integrators and payment processors, including UltraFICO with Plaid [1]. Profitability moved sharply higher, with a gross margin of 86.1% and diluted EPS of $36.32, up 37% [1]. The company holds 206 U.S. and 37 foreign patents, which supports the franchise but does not shield it from regulatory change [1]. At a closing price of $707.40 and a market capitalisation of about $15.1 billion, the shares trade well below their 52-week high of $1,858.91 [2].
market_position:
FICO's end market is overwhelmingly financial services in the Americas. Financial services generated 92% of fiscal 2026 revenue and the Americas 89%, while about one-fifth of revenue came from outside the U.S. [1]. Customers include more than three-quarters of the 100 largest U.S. financial institutions, nearly all of the 100 largest banks worldwide, more than 600 insurers and more than 200 government agencies [1]. The filing gives no overall market share figure, so the position has to be judged from distribution and regulatory standing rather than a reported share [1].

Concentration is the defining feature of that position. Experian, TransUnion and Equifax provided 60% of revenue, up from 51% a year earlier [1]. The same three agencies distribute FICO products and also sell VantageScore, a score they own through a joint venture, to compete directly with FICO [1]. Regulatory acceptance is moving toward VantageScore. The FHFA's July 2025 lender choice regime opened the door, and in April 2026 HUD announced that the FHA would accept VantageScore alongside FICO from January 1, 2027 [1]. The company says it cannot predict how fast adoption will occur [1].

The market view is more cautious than the financials. Consensus rates the shares Hold with a target price of $814.95 (range $481.00 to $1,230.97) as of November 25, 2026, a date after the 10-K. The target sits about 15% above the $707.40 close [3][2]. Against TransUnion, Equifax and Verisk, FICO is the smallest by revenue, yet it leads on gross margin and return on invested capital, with a 2025 ROIC of 58.1% against 20.7% at Verisk and 8.5% at Equifax [4]. Its 2025 EV/EBITDA of 40.5x was about double Verisk's 20.2x, so the market is paying a clear premium for that position [4].
operating_results:
Revenue rose 27% to $2,534.9 million in fiscal 2026 from $1,990.9 million, led by Scores, which grew 41% to $1,652.2 million, while Software grew 7% to $882.7 million [1]. Cost of revenues fell 1% to $351.5 million, lifting gross margin to 86.1% from 82.2%. Operating income rose 37% to $1,265.7 million, and operating margin reached 50% from 46% [1]. The gain was strong but not clean: selling, general and administrative expense rose 33% to $681.1 million, including a $65.0 million antitrust settlement accrual [1].

Below the operating line the picture is more mixed. Interest expense rose 67% to $223.3 million on higher average debt, and the effective tax rate climbed to 24.1% from 18.8% [1]. Net income grew 28% to $835.0 million, so the net margin stayed flat at 33% [1]. Diluted EPS rose 37% to $36.32, helped by 6% fewer diluted shares [1]. Unallocated corporate expenses rose $79.5 million to $261.0 million, and restructuring charges reached $27.3 million, up from $10.9 million [1]. Scores operating income rose 45% to $1,489.9 million, while Software operating income was flat at $249.6 million [1].

Segment quality diverged. The Software margin slipped to 28% from 30%, which the filing attributes to higher third-party data center hosting costs and a $12.1 million (13%) fall in point-in-time license revenue [1]. Non-platform ARR fell 18% to $398.3 million while platform ARR rose 72% [1]. Operating cash flow rose to $1,072.1 million from $778.8 million, and free cash flow reached $1,034.4 million, though the MD&A attributes $69.8 million of the operating cash increase to timing of receipts and payments [1]. Earnings beat consensus in each of the last four quarters, by between 3.4% and 13.9% [3].
risk_assessment:
The filing's three most important risks are linked. The first is erosion of FICO Score use in U.S. mortgages. The FHFA and HUD have moved from a single-score framework to a choice regime and then toward broader acceptance of VantageScore. The filing says the Enterprises were to accept VantageScore from approved lenders in April 2026 and from all lenders in September 2026, and that the FHA would accept it from January 1, 2027, alongside FICO Score 10T [1]. The company says its stock price has declined significantly after these announcements but gives no figures, and it cannot predict how far adoption will go [1]. The filing does not size the mortgage share of Scores revenue, so this exposure cannot be quantified from the document [1].

The second risk is concentration. Banking produced 92% of fiscal 2026 revenue. The filing says banking account growth has been slow and that large customers may have sufficient bargaining power to demand reduced prices [1]. Cyclicality matters here: a downturn, higher rates or tariffs can reduce credit applications and the volume of royalty-bearing transactions [1]. The third risk is AI-driven competition and execution. The filing lists 14 categories of competitors, including large language model developers and in-house data science teams, and discloses past product delays and defects that could recur [1]. The $27.3 million restructuring charge makes the cost of that execution risk visible [1].

The balance sheet adds a financial risk. Total debt rose to $5,277.9 million from $3,074.9 million, or 4.2x operating income against 3.3x a year earlier. The company carries a stockholders' deficit of $3,873.2 million, driven by $10,539.2 million of treasury stock [1]. The current ratio improved to 0.99 from 0.83 [1]. Cash is $217.6 million, and $337.5 million of term loan principal falls due within twelve months [1]. Interest paid more than doubled to $224.4 million [1]. Yahoo-derived quality screens are reassuring, with a Piotroski score of 8 of 9, an Altman Z-score of 8.47 and a Beneish M-score of -3.10, which does not flag manipulation [2]. These are our own calculations from Yahoo statements, not company disclosures.

Forward risk shows up in estimates. Current-year EPS consensus fell 16.5% over 90 days to $44.36, and next-year EPS fell 20.6% to $50.95, with few analysts raising estimates [3]. These revisions are dated after the 10-K.
competitors_analysis:
Peer selection followed business model first and size second. TransUnion and Equifax are the closest matches: both are consumer credit-data companies, and both sell competing score or risk products. Verisk is the third peer, a data-analytics and decisioning business whose revenue of $3.2 billion is close to FICO's size [4]. Software-only names such as Tyler and PTC were closer in size but are less comparable on business model. FICO is the smallest of the four by revenue. Its fiscal 2026 revenue was $2.53 billion, while the peer candidate table lists revenue of $5.0 billion for TransUnion, $6.6 billion for Equifax and $3.2 billion for Verisk [4].

FICO's growth and margins stand out. Revenue growth accelerated from 13.5% in 2024 to 15.9% in 2025 and 27.3% in 2026, while TransUnion grew 9.4% in 2025, Equifax 6.9% and Verisk 6.6% [4]. Gross margin was 82.2% in 2025, against 59.1% at TransUnion, 56.4% at Equifax and 69.9% at Verisk [4]. EBITDA margin was 47.8% in 2025, below Verisk's 54.3% but well above TransUnion's 31.8% and Equifax's 30.2% [4]. Return on invested capital was 58.1% in 2025, against 6.7% at TransUnion, 8.5% at Equifax and 20.7% at Verisk [4]. The peer data uses fiscal labels that do not fully align, so these comparisons are approximate [4].

The valuation is where the gap is widest. FICO's 2025 EV/EBITDA of 40.48x compares with 14.31x to 20.18x for the peers [4]. The 2026 figure of 13.23x is below every peer's 2025 multiple, but the comparison crosses years, and the data provided does not explain the drop. Consensus rates the shares Hold with a target of $814.95 [3]. The fundamentals support a premium, since FICO leads on gross margin and return on capital, but they do not clearly support the full 2025 multiple. That is consistent with the reverse DCF result, which requires growth consensus does not yet forecast [2][3].

investment_theses.thesis: Scores will keep driving FICO's earnings in FY2027, because mortgage origination pricing holds even as VantageScore gains acceptance.
investment_theses.evidence: Scores revenue rose 41% to $1,652.2 million at a 90% segment margin in fiscal 2026 [1]. FHA acceptance of FICO Score 10T from January 1, 2027 supports the franchise, but consensus FY2027 revenue growth is only 2.2% [3].
investment_theses.signpost: Scores segment revenue growth stays above 5% year over year in each quarterly report through FY2027 (fiscal year ends September 30, 2027; annual report due around November 2027).
investment_theses.invalidation: Scores revenue falls year over year in any FY2027 quarter, or the FHA and Enterprises shift volume to VantageScore faster than the filing expects.

investment_theses.thesis: Leverage, not cash generation, becomes the binding constraint, so buybacks must slow or debt keeps rising.
investment_theses.evidence: Total debt rose to $5,277.9 million from $3,074.9 million. Debt is 4.2x operating income versus 3.3x a year earlier, and buybacks of $3,046.0 million exceeded free cash flow of $1,034.4 million [1][2].
investment_theses.signpost: Total debt to operating income below 4.0x and share repurchases below free cash flow in FY2027, reported with the 10-K around November 2027.
investment_theses.invalidation: Debt to operating income falls back to 3.3x or below while buybacks continue, which would show operating growth is outpacing borrowing.

investment_theses.thesis: At $707.40 the shares are priced for growth that consensus does not forecast, so the stock earns less than its 11.5% cost of capital unless revenue growth re-accelerates to around 10%.
investment_theses.evidence: The reverse DCF implies 10.2% revenue growth for ten years and an 8.6% implied return against an 11.5% WACC. Consensus revenue growth is 2.2% in FY2027 and 6.5% in FY2028, and current-year EPS estimates fell 16.5% in 90 days [2][3]. Consensus figures are dated after the 10-K.
investment_theses.signpost: FY2027 consensus revenue rises above $2,590.6 million at the next quarterly update, and the FY2027 result reported around November 2027 shows revenue growth above 10%.
investment_theses.invalidation: FY2027 revenue growth reaches 10% or more and consensus EPS is revised up, which would make the reverse DCF path plausible.

investment_theses.thesis: Software growth depends on platform migration, and the non-platform decline offsets platform gains unless the Software margin recovers.
investment_theses.evidence: Platform ARR rose 72% to $452.6 million, but non-platform ARR fell 18% to $398.3 million, and the Software margin slipped to 28% from 30% on higher hosting costs [1].
investment_theses.signpost: Total software ARR growth stays above 14%, the FY2026 rate, and the Software segment margin returns to 30% in FY2027 results reported around November 2027.
investment_theses.invalidation: Total software ARR growth falls below 10%, or the non-platform ARR decline accelerates beyond 25%.
